I have been farming in Quzhou for over fifty years, and I still manage the eight mu of land that my family kept after the children moved to the city for work. At seventy, my back is not what it used to be, but my mind is sharp, and having read agricultural extension materials and attended county training sessions over the years, I know the numbers behind my decisions. I will stick to the winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping system on all eight mu because it is the only rotation I fully trust: the wheat provides grain security and a stable buyer, while the maize fits perfectly into the narrow window after the early June harvest. I cannot afford to gamble on cotton or vegetables at my age—too much labor, too much price risk.

For the wheat, I will sow an improved variety in mid-October. The soil is still in decent shape, so I will do rotary tillage to prepare the seedbed, which is what everyone in the village does and what my own experience confirms works best here. I will put down about 50 kilograms of compound fertilizer per mu as a basal dose, which gives me roughly 18 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 5 kg of potassium per mu. I know from the county agronomists that split application is better, so I will topdress with urea at jointing if the plants look a little yellow, but I budget the total nitrogen at 18 kg per mu—high enough to push for a good yield but not so high that I waste money if the spring is dry. I will irrigate four times: once at planting to ensure germination, once at overwintering if there is no rain, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Water from the tube well is expensive, but losing a quarter of the yield because of drought at grain filling would hurt far more. I will spray pesticides four times, mainly herbicide early on and insecticide if I see aphids or armyworms, because I have seen what happens when you wait too long.

For the summer maize, time is everything. As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June, I will no-till plant a hybrid maize variety directly into the stubble. There is no time for ploughing—the window is less than a week—and my neighbors who tried rotary tillage for maize often ended up planting too late and lost yield to early frost. I will apply compound fertilizer at about 40 kg per mu at planting, giving me roughly 14 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu. Maize here does not need as much nitrogen as wheat if the wheat residue is returned, and my own records show that pushing beyond 15 kg N per mu for maize does not pay back well on my soil. I will irrigate twice: once right after planting to help emergence, and once around the big喇叭口 stage if the July rains are late. Three pesticide applications should be enough—herbicide at planting, and one or two insecticide sprays depending on what the corn borer pressure looks like in July.

I am targeting about 530 kg per mu for the wheat and 560 kg per mu for the maize. Those are realistic numbers based on what I got last year and what the better-managed plots in the village achieve. I am not chasing record yields; I am chasing stability.
